methodology: Curated policy snapshot. An enacted statute includes narrow testing or pilot laws; EO history includes rescinded orders. Secondary survey classifications require primary-text review. No-policy-record is not a finding that AV operation is legal or illegal. Dates are null when enactment date is unverified.

federal.title: FMVSS barrier review
federal.summary: NHTSA requested public input on whether federal vehicle safety standards written for human-driver controls or seating positions could pose unnecessary barriers to automated-driving vehicles. The notice sought examples of affected provisions and possible revisions but did not propose specific binding regulatory text or change any existing certification requirements.
federal.takeaway: NHTSA requested public input on whether federal vehicle safety standards written for human-driver controls or seating positions could pose unnecessary barriers to automated-driving vehicles. The notice sought examples of affected provisions and possible revisions but did not propose specific binding regulatory text or change any existing certification requirements.

federal.title: Removing regulatory barriers for ADS vehicles
federal.summary: NHTSA requested detailed input on adapting crash-avoidance safety standards for vehicles equipped with automated driving systems that may lack conventional driver controls. The advance notice explored how to preserve safety performance while rethinking driver-oriented specifications and tests; it did not itself amend any standard or authorize driverless deployment.
federal.takeaway: NHTSA requested detailed input on adapting crash-avoidance safety standards for vehicles equipped with automated driving systems that may lack conventional driver controls. The advance notice explored how to preserve safety performance while rethinking driver-oriented specifications and tests; it did not itself amend any standard or authorize driverless deployment.

federal.title: Occupant protection proposal
federal.summary: NHTSA proposed revising eleven occupant crash-protection standards to accommodate automated-driving vehicles without conventional steering wheels and driver seats. Proposed changes would revise seat terminology, crash-test references, steering-system applicability and protections for occupantless cargo vehicles. NHTSA later finalized a revised package affecting thirteen standards in March 2022.
federal.takeaway: NHTSA proposed revising eleven occupant crash-protection standards to accommodate automated-driving vehicles without conventional steering wheels and driver seats. Proposed changes would revise seat terminology, crash-test references, steering-system applicability and protections for occupantless cargo vehicles. NHTSA later finalized a revised package affecting thirteen standards in March 2022.

federal.title: Occupant protection final rule
federal.summary: NHTSA amended thirteen occupant protection standards for vehicles equipped with automated driving systems and lacking traditional human driving controls. The March 2022 final rule updates driver-seat and steering references, test procedures and selected applicability provisions while retaining crash protections for passengers; it does not establish automated-driving performance or operational safety standards.
federal.takeaway: NHTSA amended thirteen occupant protection standards for vehicles equipped with automated driving systems and lacking traditional human driving controls. The March 2022 final rule updates driver-seat and steering references, test procedures and selected applicability provisions while retaining crash protections for passengers; it does not establish automated-driving performance or operational safety standards.

federal.title: Steering control rearward displacement · FMVSS 204
federal.summary: NHTSA's final rule exempts vehicles certified to Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 208's frontal-barrier crash-protection provisions from the steering-column rearward displacement test of Standard 204. This generally applicable vehicle-design amendment removes obsolete requirements; it is separate from the 2022 change for automated vehicles with no steering column.
federal.takeaway: NHTSA's final rule exempts vehicles certified to Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 208's frontal-barrier crash-protection provisions from the steering-column rearward displacement test of Standard 204. This generally applicable vehicle-design amendment removes obsolete requirements; it is separate from the 2022 change for automated vehicles with no steering column.

federal.title: Transmission displays · FMVSS 102
federal.summary: NHTSA proposes to exempt vehicles equipped with automated driving systems and no manual driving controls from the requirement to display transmission shift positions to a human driver. The proposal addresses human-facing transmission indicators, not the vehicle's underlying transmission safety or automated driving performance.
federal.takeaway: NHTSA proposes to exempt vehicles equipped with automated driving systems and no manual driving controls from the requirement to display transmission shift positions to a human driver. The proposal addresses human-facing transmission indicators, not the vehicle's underlying transmission safety or automated driving performance.

federal.title: Defrosting and windshield wiping · FMVSS 103/104
federal.summary: NHTSA proposes to exempt vehicles designed for automated driving without conventional manual driving controls from selected windshield defrosting, defogging, wiping, and washing requirements intended to maintain a human driver's view. The proposal covers Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards 103 and 104; it is not yet an adopted exemption.
federal.takeaway: NHTSA proposes to exempt vehicles designed for automated driving without conventional manual driving controls from selected windshield defrosting, defogging, wiping, and washing requirements intended to maintain a human driver's view. The proposal covers Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards 103 and 104; it is not yet an adopted exemption.

federal.title: Tire placards · FMVSS 110
federal.summary: NHTSA proposes changing tire and loading information placard rules for vehicles without a conventional driver's side. Instead of requiring placement specifically on the driver's side, the proposed amendment would permit the placard on the left side of these vehicles. The proposal concerns vehicle labeling, not tire performance requirements.
federal.takeaway: NHTSA proposes changing tire and loading information placard rules for vehicles without a conventional driver's side. Instead of requiring placement specifically on the driver's side, the proposed amendment would permit the placard on the left side of these vehicles. The proposal concerns vehicle labeling, not tire performance requirements.

federal.title: Brake controls · FMVSS 135
federal.summary: NHTSA proposes removing requirements for hand- or foot-operated service-brake controls from vehicles designed to be driven exclusively by automated driving systems. It would also adapt brake warnings, parking-brake controls and test procedures for vehicles without a human driver's position, while retaining the standard's braking-performance protections.
federal.takeaway: NHTSA proposes removing requirements for hand- or foot-operated service-brake controls from vehicles designed to be driven exclusively by automated driving systems. It would also adapt brake warnings, parking-brake controls and test procedures for vehicles without a human driver's position, while retaining the standard's braking-performance protections.

federal.title: FMVSS 201 · Interior impact
federal.summary: The 2022 final rule adapts interior-impact occupant protection tests and seat-position references to vehicles without conventional steering wheels or driver seats. Requirements now use vehicle seating layouts and occupant positions, rather than assuming a human-driven left-front seat. Crashworthiness protections continue to apply wherever a vehicle is designed to carry people.
federal.takeaway: The 2022 final rule adapts interior-impact occupant protection tests and seat-position references to vehicles without conventional steering wheels or driver seats. Requirements now use vehicle seating layouts and occupant positions, rather than assuming a human-driven left-front seat. Crashworthiness protections continue to apply wherever a vehicle is designed to carry people.

federal.title: FMVSS 203 · Steering control impact
federal.summary: The rule excludes vehicles designed without steering controls from the steering-control impact standard, because there is no steering wheel or column for occupants to strike. Vehicles equipped with conventional steering controls remain subject to applicable impact requirements; this is a design-specific exemption, not a blanket waiver of occupant crash protection.
federal.takeaway: The rule excludes vehicles designed without steering controls from the steering-control impact standard, because there is no steering wheel or column for occupants to strike. Vehicles equipped with conventional steering controls remain subject to applicable impact requirements; this is a design-specific exemption, not a blanket waiver of occupant crash protection.

federal.title: FMVSS 204 · Steering control rearward displacement
federal.summary: The rule removes application of the steering-column rearward displacement test to vehicles without steering controls, where the test has no relevant component. The 2022 amendment is limited to driverless-control designs; a separate 2026 rule later addressed steering-column displacement requirements for certain vehicles certified under the frontal crash standard.
federal.takeaway: The rule removes application of the steering-column rearward displacement test to vehicles without steering controls, where the test has no relevant component. The 2022 amendment is limited to driverless-control designs; a separate 2026 rule later addressed steering-column displacement requirements for certain vehicles certified under the frontal crash standard.

federal.title: FMVSS 205 · Glazing materials
federal.summary: The final rule clarifies glazing-material requirements for vehicles built without human occupants, including an amended application to trucks designed to carry at least one person. Occupant-protection glazing requirements continue where vehicles carry people; the rule does not create new performance standards for automated driving or sensors.
federal.takeaway: The final rule clarifies glazing-material requirements for vehicles built without human occupants, including an amended application to trucks designed to carry at least one person. Occupant-protection glazing requirements continue where vehicles carry people; the rule does not create new performance standards for automated driving or sensors.

federal.title: FMVSS 206 · Door locks and retention
federal.summary: The rule revises door-lock and door-retention terminology and applicability for vehicles with no conventional driver's seat or manual steering controls. It uses physical seating and door locations instead of human-driver references, retaining relevant door-retention crash protection for passenger-carrying vehicles, including driverless designs.
federal.takeaway: The rule revises door-lock and door-retention terminology and applicability for vehicles with no conventional driver's seat or manual steering controls. It uses physical seating and door locations instead of human-driver references, retaining relevant door-retention crash protection for passenger-carrying vehicles, including driverless designs.

federal.title: FMVSS 207 · Seating systems
federal.summary: The final rule changes seating-system requirements and definitions so a vehicle is not assumed to have a designated driver's seat unless manually operated driving controls are present. Seat strength, anchorage and other relevant passenger seating protections remain in force for automated vehicles built to transport people.
federal.takeaway: The final rule changes seating-system requirements and definitions so a vehicle is not assumed to have a designated driver's seat unless manually operated driving controls are present. Seat strength, anchorage and other relevant passenger seating protections remain in force for automated vehicles built to transport people.

federal.title: FMVSS 208 · Occupant crash protection
federal.summary: The rule extensively revises occupant crash-protection terms, airbag suppression requirements, test-dummy placement and front-row seating references for vehicles without human driving controls. It clarifies protection of front-center and other inboard positions and retains occupant protection performance standards; NHTSA did not adopt a proposed child-detection vehicle-motion suppression requirement.
federal.takeaway: The rule extensively revises occupant crash-protection terms, airbag suppression requirements, test-dummy placement and front-row seating references for vehicles without human driving controls. It clarifies protection of front-center and other inboard positions and retains occupant protection performance standards; NHTSA did not adopt a proposed child-detection vehicle-motion suppression requirement.

federal.title: FMVSS 212 · Windshield mounting
federal.summary: The final rule amends windshield-mounting standard applicability to exclude trucks not designed to carry any person. Because this standard protects occupants from windshield separation during a crash, NHTSA determined it need not apply to occupantless cargo vehicles. The requirement remains applicable to passenger-carrying vehicle configurations.
federal.takeaway: The final rule amends windshield-mounting standard applicability to exclude trucks not designed to carry any person. Because this standard protects occupants from windshield separation during a crash, NHTSA determined it need not apply to occupantless cargo vehicles. The requirement remains applicable to passenger-carrying vehicle configurations.

federal.title: FMVSS 214 · Side impact protection
federal.summary: The rule replaces driver-based side-impact test references with front-row, left-side and right-side seating positions where necessary for vehicles without conventional driver controls. It preserves side-impact protection and crash-test requirements for passenger-carrying automated vehicles, adapting how tests are positioned rather than exempting the vehicle from protection.
federal.takeaway: The rule replaces driver-based side-impact test references with front-row, left-side and right-side seating positions where necessary for vehicles without conventional driver controls. It preserves side-impact protection and crash-test requirements for passenger-carrying automated vehicles, adapting how tests are positioned rather than exempting the vehicle from protection.

federal.title: FMVSS 216a · Roof crush resistance
federal.summary: The rule revises roof-crush resistance terminology, applicability and seating/test-location references for vehicles without traditional driver seats or steering controls. Passenger-carrying automated vehicles remain subject to relevant roof-strength protections, while requirements designed to protect occupants are not applied indiscriminately to vehicles built to carry no people.
federal.takeaway: The rule revises roof-crush resistance terminology, applicability and seating/test-location references for vehicles without traditional driver seats or steering controls. Passenger-carrying automated vehicles remain subject to relevant roof-strength protections, while requirements designed to protect occupants are not applied indiscriminately to vehicles built to carry no people.

federal.title: FMVSS 219 · Windshield zone intrusion
federal.summary: NHTSA changed the windshield-zone intrusion standard to exclude trucks designed to carry no person. The rule recognizes that its purpose is to prevent injuries to occupants from components intruding into the windshield area during a crash. Passenger-carrying automated vehicles still must meet applicable intrusion requirements.
federal.takeaway: NHTSA changed the windshield-zone intrusion standard to exclude trucks designed to carry no person. The rule recognizes that its purpose is to prevent injuries to occupants from components intruding into the windshield area during a crash. Passenger-carrying automated vehicles still must meet applicable intrusion requirements.

federal.title: FMVSS 225 · Child restraint anchorages
federal.summary: The final rule revises the shuttle-bus definition for child-restraint anchorage requirements. In a bus without manually operated driving controls, the single rearward row of forward-facing seats is now referenced relative to all front-row passenger seats, rather than a nonexistent driver's seat; existing applicable child-restraint provisions remain.
federal.takeaway: The final rule revises the shuttle-bus definition for child-restraint anchorage requirements. In a bus without manually operated driving controls, the single rearward row of forward-facing seats is now referenced relative to all front-row passenger seats, rather than a nonexistent driver's seat; existing applicable child-restraint provisions remain.

federal.title: FMVSS 226 · Ejection mitigation
federal.summary: The rule revises ejection-mitigation applicability, roof and seat-reference definitions and certain test procedures for vehicles without conventional driving controls. NHTSA did not finalize changes to the ejection-mitigation readiness indicator, leaving that issue for a separate potential rulemaking; protection continues for vehicles built to carry people.
federal.takeaway: The rule revises ejection-mitigation applicability, roof and seat-reference definitions and certain test procedures for vehicles without conventional driving controls. NHTSA did not finalize changes to the ejection-mitigation readiness indicator, leaving that issue for a separate potential rulemaking; protection continues for vehicles built to carry people.

federal_oversight.title: Standing General Order crash reporting
federal_oversight.summary: NHTSA's June 29, 2021 order required named automated-driving and Level 2 driver-assistance developers and operators to report public-road crashes when the system was engaged within 30 seconds. Crashes with a hospital trip, fatality, tow-away, air bag deployment or vulnerable road user were due within one day with a 10-day update; other ADS crashes were monthly. Reports do not establish fault.
federal_oversight.takeaway: NHTSA's June 29, 2021 order required named automated-driving and Level 2 driver-assistance developers and operators to report public-road crashes when the system was engaged within 30 seconds. Crashes with a hospital trip, fatality, tow-away, air bag deployment or vulnerable road user were due within one day with a 10-day update; other ADS crashes were monthly. Reports do not establish fault.

federal_oversight.title: Third amended Standing General Order
federal_oversight.summary: Effective June 16, 2025, NHTSA's third amended crash-reporting order requires covered operators and manufacturers to report serious automated-driving or Level 2 driver-assistance crashes within five days and qualifying less-serious crashes monthly. It differentiates reporting thresholds by automation type, reduces duplicate filings, and requires updates when new information becomes available.
federal_oversight.takeaway: Effective June 16, 2025, NHTSA's third amended crash-reporting order requires covered operators and manufacturers to report serious automated-driving or Level 2 driver-assistance crashes within five days and qualifying less-serious crashes monthly. It differentiates reporting thresholds by automation type, reduces duplicate filings, and requires updates when new information becomes available.

federal_oversight.title: AV STEP proposal
federal_oversight.summary: NHTSA proposed a voluntary program in which ADS developers, manufacturers and fleet operators would apply for admission, submit independent safety assessments, and accept periodic and event-triggered reporting and public disclosure. It offered two participation levels, including new exemptions for vehicles not meeting all safety standards; comments closed March 17, 2025, and NHTSA withdrew the proposal on June 26, 2026.
federal_oversight.takeaway: NHTSA proposed a voluntary program in which ADS developers, manufacturers and fleet operators would apply for admission, submit independent safety assessments, and accept periodic and event-triggered reporting and public disclosure. It offered two participation levels, including new exemptions for vehicles not meeting all safety standards; comments closed March 17, 2025, and NHTSA withdrew the proposal on June 26, 2026.

federal_oversight.title: AV STEP withdrawal
federal_oversight.summary: NHTSA withdrew its January 2025 AV STEP proposal on June 26, 2026, after 37 comments argued the voluntary program was complex, unattractive to potential participants and insufficient for oversight. NHTSA added that exemption improvements under its April 2025 AV Framework had already advanced some of the proposal's goals.
federal_oversight.takeaway: NHTSA withdrew its January 2025 AV STEP proposal on June 26, 2026, after 37 comments argued the voluntary program was complex, unattractive to potential participants and insufficient for oversight. NHTSA added that exemption improvements under its April 2025 AV Framework had already advanced some of the proposal's goals.

federal_oversight.title: FMCSA grants Aurora warning-beacon exemption
federal_oversight.summary: FMCSA published a notice of final disposition granting Aurora Operations, Inc. a limited five-year exemption for Level 4 automated driving system trucks, allowing cab-mounted warning beacons in place of traditional warning devices. Effective October 7, 2026 through October 7, 2031.
federal_oversight.takeaway: FMCSA published a notice of final disposition granting Aurora Operations, Inc. a limited five-year exemption for Level 4 automated driving system trucks, allowing cab-mounted warning beacons in place of traditional warning devices. Effective October 7, 2026 through October 7, 2031.

federal_oversight.title: NHTSA grants Zoox temporary FMVSS exemption
federal_oversight.summary: NHTSA granted Zoox, Inc. a temporary exemption from portions of eight Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards for its automated-driving-system-equipped vehicle, subject to conditions including enhanced oversight. The exemption runs July 31, 2026 through July 31, 2028.
federal_oversight.takeaway: NHTSA granted Zoox, Inc. a temporary exemption from portions of eight Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards for its automated-driving-system-equipped vehicle, subject to conditions including enhanced oversight. The exemption runs July 31, 2026 through July 31, 2028.

federal_oversight.title: NHTSA AV Framework interim exemption guidance
federal_oversight.summary: NHTSA published a notice of updates under its AV Framework and requested public comment on interim guidance for commercial deployment exemptions for automated vehicles; the notice set an August 31, 2026 comment deadline (a later notice, 2026-17741, extended it).
federal_oversight.takeaway: NHTSA published a notice of updates under its AV Framework and requested public comment on interim guidance for commercial deployment exemptions for automated vehicles; the notice set an August 31, 2026 comment deadline (a later notice, 2026-17741, extended it).

federal_oversight.title: NHTSA plans updated ADS guidance
federal_oversight.summary: NHTSA gave notice of public availability and requested comment on its intent to issue comprehensive updated guidance on safe development and deployment of automated driving systems, releasing draft chapters for comment and later consolidating them into a final document. Comments are due by July 31, 2027.
federal_oversight.takeaway: NHTSA gave notice of public availability and requested comment on its intent to issue comprehensive updated guidance on safe development and deployment of automated driving systems, releasing draft chapters for comment and later consolidating them into a final document. Comments are due by July 31, 2027.

federal_oversight.title: NHTSA fall 2026 research meeting and ADS workshop
federal_oversight.summary: NHTSA announced a public meeting on December 1-2, 2026 on its safety research programs. On the afternoon of December 1 the Office of Automation Safety will convene an Automated Driving Systems workshop, which will not be recorded.
federal_oversight.takeaway: NHTSA announced a public meeting on December 1-2, 2026 on its safety research programs. On the afternoon of December 1 the Office of Automation Safety will convene an Automated Driving Systems workshop, which will not be recorded.

states.name: Alabama
states.analysis: Alabama's 2019 SB 47 authorizes driverless operation only for automated commercial vehicles, with a $2 million liability minimum, owner-as-operator liability and a bar on AV-specific local or state requirements. It does not create a passenger robotaxi pathway.
states.oversight: Alabama DOT has state-level jurisdiction under the commercial vehicle framework.

states.name: Alaska
states.framework: No enacted AV operation framework identified
states.analysis: Proposals to restrict autonomous operation and assign operator liability remained under consideration in the 2026 survey. Proposed bills are not current operating authority.
states.oversight: General motor vehicle law applies while the proposed AV measures remain unenacted.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: Arizona
states.analysis: Arizona allows driverless operation under HB 2813 (2021, A.R.S. § 28-9702) once an operator files a law-enforcement interaction plan and a written acknowledgment of federal, traffic, insurance and registration compliance; ADOT can issue a cease-and-desist letter if either is missing. The statute builds on 2015 and 2018 executive orders. A company operating in Arizona does not have statewide service coverage.
states.oversight: Arizona MVD notification and certification.
states.source_label: Arizona DOT AV framework and HB 2813 history

states.name: Arkansas
states.analysis: Arkansas Act 468 (2019) allows autonomous and fully autonomous vehicles only under a pilot program approved by the State Highway Commission, which is deemed approved 60 days after submission. The program must state its commercial purpose and insurance needs, and no more than three vehicles may operate at once.
states.oversight: State submission and applicable traffic and vehicle rules.

states.name: California
states.analysis: California regulates AVs in two tracks. The DMV (Vehicle Code § 38750, Articles 3.7 and 3.8) issues testing with a driver, driverless testing and deployment permits and collects collision reports; the CPUC separately authorizes passenger service. A DMV permit alone does not authorize paid rides.
states.oversight: DMV: vehicle testing, deployment permits and reporting. CPUC: passenger service pilots, fare-charging deployment, passenger safety and service reporting.

states.name: Colorado
states.framework: AV operating framework; truck restrictions vetoed
states.analysis: Colorado's SB 17-213 (2017) makes automated-driving-system regulation a statewide concern, bars local standards that differ from those for human drivers, and authorizes systems that can follow every state and federal driving law. A system that cannot must get Colorado State Patrol and CDOT approval before testing.
states.oversight: State motor vehicle law and any applicable testing conditions.

states.name: Connecticut
states.analysis: Connecticut's Public Act 17-69 (2017) is a pilot, not statewide authority: up to four municipalities may host fully autonomous vehicle testing under agreements fixing routes and hours, with at least $5 million in insurance, self-insurance or bond. A task force studies fully autonomous vehicles and the pilot reports annually.
states.oversight: Pilot approval and participating municipalities.

states.name: Delaware
states.framework: No enacted AV-specific operating statute identified
states.analysis: Delaware's 2025 proposal to require an onboard operator failed. Its AV advisory activity does not itself grant a commercial permit.
states.oversight: Ordinary vehicle rules; no distinct statewide commercial AV permit identified in the guide.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: Florida
states.analysis: Florida Statutes § 316.85 allows driverless operation with no person physically present and treats the automated driving system as the operator. On-demand networks must meet § 627.749 insurance requirements, and local governments may not add taxes, fees or other requirements, though airports and seaports may charge reasonable fees.
states.oversight: Vehicle registration and statutory operating requirements.

states.name: Georgia
states.analysis: Georgia's SB 219 (2017) allows a fully autonomous vehicle to operate with no human driver if it meets federal standards, can reach a minimal-risk condition, is registered as such and has liability coverage meeting the state minimum. Driver licensing does not apply. The statute does not show where any operator actually runs.
states.oversight: State motor vehicle law and applicable service regulation.

states.name: Hawaii
states.analysis: Hawaii Act 21 (2020) is a testing pilot run by the Department of Transportation, allowing testing on public roads only with a human driver physically present to intervene. The department decides which entities may test, and the pilot did not grant general driverless commercial authority.
states.oversight: Hawaii DOT determined eligible pilot testers.

states.name: Idaho
states.analysis: Idaho's executive-order committee examined testing and deployment issues. The 2026 survey identified no enacted AV-specific operating statute.
states.oversight: General motor vehicle requirements and agency guidance.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: Illinois
states.analysis: Illinois Vehicle Code § 11-208(e-10) bars local governments, including home-rule units, from prohibiting automated-driving-system vehicles or regulating them inconsistently with the Vehicle Code, while keeping local traffic control. It is a preemption rule, not a statewide permit or deployment framework.
states.oversight: State vehicle and traffic law; local powers are constrained by statute.

states.name: Indiana
states.framework: No enacted AV-specific operating statute identified
states.analysis: Indiana's 2025 bill addressing autonomous tractor-trailers failed. The 2026 survey did not identify a dedicated AV operating law.
states.oversight: Ordinary vehicle and commercial-carrier requirements.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: Iowa
states.analysis: Iowa Code §§ 321.514–321.519 (2019 SF 302) authorize driverless-capable vehicles and give the Department of Transportation rulemaking authority. Under the department's rules, Level 4 and 5 vehicles do not need a conventional human driver and registrants must say whether a vehicle is driverless-capable.
states.oversight: State traffic and vehicle requirements under Iowa's AV statute.

states.name: Kansas
states.analysis: Kansas K.S.A. 8-2902 allows driverless-capable vehicles to operate without a human driver if they can reach a minimal-risk condition, follow traffic laws and carry required federal labels, with a law-enforcement interaction plan on file with the Highway Patrol. A human driver must be present for a vehicle's first 12 months in Kansas service, except vehicles not designed for people.
states.oversight: State vehicle and traffic rules.

states.name: Kentucky
states.analysis: Kentucky's HB 7 (2024) creates a fully autonomous vehicle framework administered by the Transportation Cabinet, requiring $1 million in insurance, registration and a law-enforcement interaction plan, with limits on local regulation. Vehicles over 62,000 pounds needed a credentialed human driver until July 31, 2026.
states.oversight: State vehicle law and any remaining commercial-carrier requirements.

states.name: Louisiana
states.analysis: Louisiana R.S. 32:400.3 (Act 232 of 2019) lets autonomous commercial motor vehicles operate with no driver in the vehicle if they meet federal and state requirements and carry at least $2 million in coverage. The authority covers commercial vehicles only, so passenger service cannot be inferred from it.
states.oversight: State commercial-vehicle and traffic requirements.

states.name: Maine
states.analysis: Maine has no driverless-operation statute: Resolve Chapter 46 created a Commission on Autonomous Vehicles and directed the Department of Transportation to set up a process authorizing AV testers to demonstrate and deploy automated driving systems for testing on public ways. The commissioner can halt testing that threatens public safety.
states.oversight: Maine DOT pilot rules and general vehicle requirements.

states.name: Maryland
states.analysis: Maryland Transportation Article §§ 15-901 to 15-903 cover only commercial or industrial vehicles and mainly let autonomous vehicle converters sell or lease aftermarket-converted vehicles without a dealer or manufacturer license. They do not set general rules for driverless operation on public roads.
states.oversight: Motor Vehicle Administration and applicable vehicle law.

states.name: Massachusetts
states.analysis: Executive Order 572 established a testing framework in 2016 and was rescinded by Executive Order 603 in 2022. Current testing authority needs separate verification.
states.oversight: Do not rely on the rescinded order for current testing.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: Michigan
states.analysis: Michigan Vehicle Code § 257.665 allows manufacturers and upfitters of automated driving systems to research and test automated vehicles on public roads, with or without a human operator, after showing insurance and minimal-risk capability. The engaged system counts as the driver, and § 257.665c lets the state designate automated vehicle roadways and preempts conflicting local ordinances.
states.oversight: State AV statutes and vehicle rules.

states.name: Minnesota
states.framework: No comprehensive AV operation law enacted
states.analysis: Minnesota proposed an AV and on-demand network framework in 2026, but it failed. The proposal should not be represented as an active permit system.
states.oversight: General vehicle rules and any relevant agency guidance.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: Mississippi
states.analysis: Mississippi's MS FAVE Act (HB 1003, 2023, effective July 1, 2023) allows fully autonomous vehicles without a human driver, with proof of financial responsibility, state registration and titling, and a law enforcement interaction plan whose section is written to be repealed July 1, 2026. State agencies and localities may not add AV-specific taxes, fees or requirements.
states.oversight: State traffic, registration, and safety requirements.

states.name: Missouri
states.analysis: A Missouri proposal requiring an active human driver was still pending in the survey. Its introduction alone does not change current AV operating law.
states.oversight: General state motor vehicle and carrier rules.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: Montana
states.analysis: Montana Code § 61-6-409 (2025) allows Level 1–3 automated driving systems on public highways and Level 4–5 vehicles subject to limits set by Department of Transportation rulemaking. Cities may regulate traffic but cannot discriminate against vehicles with automated driving systems.
states.oversight: State vehicle and commercial-carrier requirements.

states.name: Nebraska
states.analysis: Nebraska Revised Statute 60-3302 (LB 989, 2018) permits driverless-capable vehicles on public roads with no human driver if they can reach a minimal risk condition and comply with state traffic law, including at railroad crossings, unless the department grants an exemption.
states.oversight: State statutory requirements for driverless operation and ordinary vehicle law.

states.name: Nevada
states.analysis: Nevada's DMV runs a self-certification system under NRS chapters 482A and 482B: applicants register for testing with bond and insurance, then certify specific make, model and year vehicles for operation. The DMV does not test or certify the technology, and 2011 AB 511 and 2017 AB 69 built the statutory base.
states.oversight: Nevada DMV testing and operation certification.

states.name: New Hampshire
states.framework: Testing pilot and conditional driverless operation
states.analysis: New Hampshire RSA 242:1 sets up a DMV pilot for testing automated vehicles, with $5 million in financial responsibility and a $500 annual fee, and also allows driverless-capable vehicles and on-demand driverless networks on public roads under conditions on minimal risk, traffic law, federal rules and insurance.
states.oversight: Pilot approval and commission reporting.

states.name: New Jersey
states.analysis: A 2026 bill proposed a fully autonomous vehicle pilot. The guide identifies it as pending, so a proposed pilot cannot be shown as active authorization.
states.oversight: General motor vehicle rules pending enacted AV legislation.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: New Mexico
states.framework: Statute with NMDOT notification and certification rule
states.analysis: New Mexico regulates AVs under a 2021 statute (HB 270, NMSA 66-7-13) and an NMDOT rule (18.24.1.9 NMAC, April 2022): owners notify NMDOT before public-road testing, vehicles meet federal and traffic law, and fully driverless testing needs a submitted testing statement and certification. Local bans based solely on automation are barred. Later bills adding human-operator requirements (HB 378, HB 148) were not confirmed enacted.
states.oversight: State transportation and testing-notification requirements.

states.name: New York
states.framework: State demonstration permit; additional NYC test permit
states.analysis: New York has no permanent AV statute; the DMV runs a demonstration and testing permit program that requires a licensed person in the driver's seat, a law enforcement interaction plan and $5 million in insurance, under a law the DMV says expires April 1, 2028. Testing in New York City also needs a separate NYC DOT permit.
states.oversight: NYS DMV demonstration program; NYC DOT testing permit within the city.
states.source_label: New York State DMV AV demonstration

states.name: North Carolina
states.analysis: North Carolina G.S. 20-400 to 20-402 (2017) lets fully autonomous vehicles operate without a licensed driver if they meet federal standards, can reach a minimal risk condition, are registered as fully autonomous and are insured. The registered owner answers for moving violations and localities cannot regulate these vehicles separately.
states.oversight: State traffic law and committee-led policy review.

states.name: North Dakota
states.analysis: North Dakota Century Code § 39-01-01.2 allows an autonomous vehicle to operate without a human driver if it can reach a minimal risk condition after a system failure and meets registration, title and insurance rules. A person using the vehicle is not driving it and needs no license; existing liability law is unchanged.
states.oversight: Ordinary vehicle law plus the state's AV operating provision.

states.name: Ohio
states.analysis: Ohio's DriveOhio program requires companies to register before AV testing. The guide identifies no general AV operation statute; registration should not be read as commercial deployment approval.
states.oversight: DriveOhio testing registration and state vehicle rules.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: Oklahoma
states.analysis: Oklahoma SB 1541 (2022) allows fully autonomous vehicles without a human driver once a law enforcement interaction plan is filed with the Department of Public Safety and at least $1,000,000 in insurance or self-insurance is shown. On-demand networks follow the Transportation Network Company Service Act.
states.oversight: State traffic, registration, and on-demand network requirements.

states.name: Oregon
states.framework: Task force, no general operating law
states.analysis: Oregon established an AV task force. A 2026 proposal to permit operation without ordinary driving privileges failed.
states.oversight: General vehicle law while broader AV operation proposals remain unenacted.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: Pennsylvania
states.analysis: Pennsylvania Title 75 Chapter 85 (Acts 117 of 2018 and 130 of 2022) makes PennDOT the lead agency and requires a certificate of compliance based on self-certification before operating highly automated vehicles, with or without a driver. The certificate holder is treated as the driver for violations and local rules are preempted.
states.oversight: PennDOT self-certification and state traffic requirements.

states.name: Rhode Island
states.framework: No dedicated AV operating law identified
states.analysis: The 2026 survey identifies no AV-specific statute or new proposal. That does not establish that an individual deployment is authorized.
states.oversight: General motor vehicle and service rules.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: South Carolina
states.framework: No dedicated AV operating law identified
states.analysis: South Carolina's survey entry identifies no new AV legislation since 2018. Operator status still depends on general vehicle law and any service-specific rules.
states.oversight: General state motor vehicle requirements.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: South Dakota
states.analysis: South Dakota HB 1095 (2024) lets fully autonomous vehicles operate with no human driver if the system is engaged and can reach a minimal risk condition and follow traffic law. The system is the driver, violations are imputed to the owner, vehicles must be insured and report their autonomy level, and localities may not add AV-specific rules.
states.oversight: State AV, commercial-carrier, and traffic rules.

states.name: Tennessee
states.analysis: Tennessee's Automated Vehicles Act (Public Chapter 474, 2017) lets ADS-operated vehicles run with no human driver if they meet federal standards, can reach a minimal risk condition and are registered as ADS-operated. Its $5 million insurance requirement was written to sunset July 1, 2021, and political subdivisions may not prohibit or regulate these vehicles.
states.oversight: State traffic law and the Automated Vehicles Act.

states.name: Texas
states.analysis: Texas SB 2205 (2017) authorized driverless operation under Transportation Code ch. 545 subch. J. SB 2807 (2025) made the automated driving system the operator and requires TxDMV authorization for commercial driverless operation, enforceable from May 28, 2026 per TxDMV. Local regulation remains barred. Authorization is a state permit, not a service area.
states.oversight: TxDMV commercial authorization; traffic-law and insurance requirements.

states.name: Utah
states.analysis: Utah Code Title 41 ch. 26 allows Level 3 vehicles under traffic-law and registration conditions and Level 4–5 vehicles to run driverless if they follow traffic law, meet federal standards and can reach a minimal risk condition. The system is the operator, owners must register and insure the vehicle, and localities cannot add AV-specific requirements.
states.oversight: State AV statute and ordinary traffic requirements.

states.name: Vermont
states.analysis: Vermont's Automated Vehicle Testing Act (23 V.S.A. ch. 41) covers testing only: testers need a Traffic Committee permit after a public hearing, an operator ready to take control, and at least $5 million in coverage. It is not a driverless passenger-service pathway.
states.oversight: Test-specific approval and public-comment process.

states.name: Virginia
states.analysis: Virginia considered autonomous operation licenses in SB 670, but the measure was continued to 2027 in the survey. Its proposed licenses are not existing permits.
states.oversight: General vehicle law pending any enacted AV-specific licensing framework.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: Washington
states.analysis: Washington regulates AV testing through Executive Order 17-02 and Department of Licensing self-certification rather than a statute. Companies need proof of insurance and an umbrella policy of at least $5,000,000 per occurrence and must file an annual collision report; self-certification is separate from vehicle registration.
states.oversight: State testing self-certification and vehicle registration processes.

states.name: West Virginia
states.analysis: West Virginia's Fully Autonomous Vehicle Act (W. Va. Code ch. 17H) allows driverless operation when the system is engaged, can reach a minimal risk condition, follows traffic law and bears federal certification labels, and covers commercial vehicles and on-demand networks. The Department of Transportation is the sole implementing agency and local AV-specific rules are barred.
states.oversight: State vehicle rules and law-enforcement interaction plan.
states.source_label: West Virginia Fully Autonomous Vehicle Act

states.name: Wisconsin
states.analysis: Wisconsin's AV steering committee addressed testing and deployment policy. Proposed 2026 board and permit legislation failed, leaving no such new permit in force.
states.oversight: General vehicle rules and existing agency coordination.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: Wyoming
states.analysis: The 2026 guide identifies no AV-specific operating law or new proposal in Wyoming. That finding does not amount to a positive authorization for any proposed service.
states.oversight: General motor vehicle and commercial-carrier rules.
states.source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

states.name: District of Columbia
states.analysis: D.C. allows only testing of vehicles with automated driving systems: testing needs an operator behind the wheel ready to take over, 10 business days' notice to DDOT and crash reporting. A testing allowance is not authorization for commercial deployment.
states.oversight: DDOT oversight.
states.source_label: DDOT AV law and testing guidance

The owner is treated as the operator, and state agencies and localities may not add AV-specific requirements, taxes or standards. It covers commercial vehicles only.

ADOT can issue a cease-and-desist letter if either is missing, and the automated system is treated as the driver.

Systems capable of conforming to every state and federal driving law are authorized; a system that cannot must obtain approval from the Colorado State Patrol and the Department of Transportation before testing.

It also created a task force to study fully autonomous vehicles and requires annual pilot reports.

state_events.title: Delaware Executive Order 14
state_events.summary: Governor Carney's Executive Order 14 (September 5, 2017) created a 19-member Advisory Council on Connected and Autonomous Vehicles of state officials, industry, legislators, planners and universities. It was to recommend tools and strategies on economic development, technology security and privacy, transportation infrastructure and public safety, reporting to the Governor and General Assembly by September 2018.

state_events.summary: Florida Statutes § 316.85 provides that a fully autonomous vehicle may operate without a licensed human operator or any person physically present, and treats the automated driving system as the operator while engaged. On-demand autonomous vehicle networks must meet the insurance requirements of § 627.749, and local governments may not impose taxes, fees or other requirements on these systems, though airports and seaports may charge reasonable fees.

state_events.title: Enacted AV Statute · Current Framework
state_events.summary: Georgia's 2017 law (SB 219) lets a fully autonomous vehicle operate with no human driver present if it meets federal safety standards, can reach a minimal-risk condition after a system failure, is registered as such, and carries liability coverage at least equal to the state minimum (250 percent of it until the end of 2019). It exempts such operation from driver licensing and treats staying on scene and calling police as accident-duty compliance.

state_events.title: Act 21 · AV testing pilot
state_events.summary: Hawaii Act 21 (approved September 15, 2020) created an autonomous vehicles testing pilot program in the Department of Transportation, allowing testing on any public road if a conventional human driver stays physically present to intervene. The department decides which entities may test and may adopt rules, and had to report before the 2023 session on whether autonomous vehicles are ready for full deployment in Hawaii.

state_events.title: Idaho Executive Order 2018-01
state_events.summary: Governor Otter's Executive Order 2018-01 (January 2, 2018) created an Autonomous and Connected Vehicle Testing and Deployment Committee, chaired by the Transportation Department director, with agency, legislative and industry members. It was to identify laws that impede testing and deployment and coordinate agencies on registration, licensing, insurance and liability, with a first report due to the Governor by November 1, 2018.

state_events.title: Enacted AV Statute · Current Framework
state_events.summary: Illinois Vehicle Code § 11-208(e-10) bars local governments, including home-rule units, from enacting ordinances that prohibit automated-driving-system vehicles on their roads or that regulate them inconsistently with the Vehicle Code, while preserving local authority over traffic control. It is a local-preemption rule rather than a licensing or deployment framework.

state_events.title: Illinois Executive Order 2018-13
state_events.summary: Executive Order 2018-13 (October 25, 2018) launched the Autonomous Illinois initiative, led by the Department of Transportation, which must review best practices, identify laws that impede testing, plan workforce training and run a testing program. Participants need a licensed driver in the vehicle and an annual notice to IDOT, which can suspend unsafe participants; IDOT reports to the Governor each June 30 and December 31.

state_events.title: Enacted AV Statute · Current Framework
state_events.summary: Iowa's 2019 SF 302 enacted Iowa Code §§ 321.514–321.519, authorizing driverless-capable vehicles on Iowa roads and giving the Department of Transportation rulemaking authority. Under the department's rules, Level 4 and 5 vehicles do not require a conventional human driver, registrants must say whether a vehicle is driverless-capable, and manufacturers supply operational-design-domain information.

state_events.summary: Kansas law (K.S.A. 8-2902) lets driverless-capable vehicles operate without a human driver if they can reach a minimal-risk condition, follow traffic laws and carry required federal labels, and the owner files a law-enforcement interaction plan with the Highway Patrol. A human driver must be present for the first 12 months a vehicle is in service in Kansas, except vehicles not designed for people, and a 34,000-pound limit applied until July 1, 2025.

state_events.summary: Kentucky's HB 7 (2024, Acts Chapter 176) established a framework for fully autonomous vehicles administered solely by the Transportation Cabinet. It requires $1 million in insurance, titling and registration and a law-enforcement interaction plan, treats the owner as operator, and limits local regulation; vehicles over 62,000 pounds needed a credentialed human driver until July 31, 2026.

state_events.summary: Louisiana R.S. 32:400.3 (Act 232 of 2019) lets an autonomous commercial motor vehicle operate without a conventional driver in the vehicle if it complies with federal and state traffic law, is registered and titled, carries federal FMVSS certification, can reach a minimal risk condition, and has at least $2 million in liability coverage. Before driverless operation, the operator must file a written certification with the state transportation department. Commercial vehicles only.

state_events.summary: Maine Resolve Chapter 46 (128th Legislature) is not a driverless-operation statute: it created a Commission on Autonomous Vehicles and directed the Commissioner of Transportation to adopt routine technical rules for evaluating and authorizing AV testers to demonstrate and deploy automated driving systems on public ways.
